locations.depot: stock we hold at a depot in Gympie itself, topped up from the Cornubia yard when a particular size or grade is not standing locally

locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft and for the drives that fall away off the ridge streets
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Gympie. Stock held locally, inspection by arrangement, and straight advice on steep drives and Mary River siting.
locations.line: We hold stock in Gympie, so a container for a Gympie address does not have to start its life on a truck three hundred kilometres south. That is worth more than it sounds when you want one this week. The awkward part is the town. Gympie was laid out around gold rather than around trucks, so the streets follow the gullies and the ridges instead of a grid, and a good half of the residential blocks fall away hard from the kerb. Add the Mary and where you put the thing matters as much as which one you buy.
locations.uses: hay, fencing wire and machinery parts on the beef and dairy country through the Mary Valley, dry storage for the macadamia and small crop growers around Amamoor, Kandanga and Imbil, timber and tool storage for the forestry and harvesting contractors working out of Curra, Glastonbury and Wolvi, boats, crab pots and dive gear at Tin Can Bay and Rainbow Beach where the garage gave up years ago, site stores on the new builds at Southside and Jones Hill, and household storage while a Queenslander at Monkland or One Mile gets restumped and reclad
access: Gympie divides into ridge and river, and the two want different trucks. The high ground — Victory Heights, Jones Hill, The Palms, the top end of Monkland — is where most of the housing sits, and it got that way because the flats were never a safe bet. Those streets were pushed through gullies and the driveways come off them at a pitch a car takes without noticing and a loaded tilt-tray does not. Where a drive drops sharply at the kerb, the back of the bed touches bitumen before the container has slid clear. Where it crests halfway up, the same thing happens in the middle instead of at the start. On a lot of those blocks the sensible answer is to lift over the fence from the street rather than try to back in. The old town on the flat is the opposite complaint: short frontages, side accesses set out long before anyone owned a car, and fifty years of fig and camphor laurel hanging over the road at exactly truck height. Out through the Mary Valley it turns rural again — Kandanga, Amamoor, Imbil, Widgee, Glastonbury — with unsealed drives that have a crown and table drains, private grids nobody can put a rating to, and turning space at the far end that needs to be real rather than hopeful. Ground varies enormously over short distances here. Down on the flats it is river silt, firm in September and treacherous a week into February. Up on the ridges it is shallow soil over rock, which carries anything you like and is almost never level. Neither stops a delivery, but both change how the unit gets bedded down. Tell us the street, what the last hundred metres looks like and whether it is sealed, and we will have the truck and the size settled before anything is booked.

sections.h: Stock on the ground in Gympie
p: We keep containers at a depot in Gympie, which is not something most sellers quoting this postcode can say. It changes two things. The first is timing — a unit already standing in town can be on your block inside a day or two rather than waiting on a slot in a run coming up the Bruce. The second is that you can lay eyes on it. Inspection is by arrangement rather than a walk-in, because the yard is not set up or staffed for the public, so ring and we will book a time and have someone there. What we will not do is print an address on a website and let you drive to a locked gate on a Saturday.

What is standing locally moves from week to week, so the honest answer on grade and size is that it depends. If you want something specific — a high cube instead of a standard, a double-door unit, a particular grade — say so when you ring. Sometimes it is already in Gympie. Sometimes it comes up on the next run and adds a few days to the date. You will be told which of those two it is, in plain terms, at the quote. If you cannot get to an inspection, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and we will send them through before delivery. Those are photos of the unit that is coming to you rather than a stock shot of something similar — corners, door end, roof and the length of the floor. It takes us two minutes and it saves a difficult conversation on the morning the truck arrives.

sections.h: The Mary, and where the box ought to sit
p: Gympie has been through more floods than anyone here needs reminding of, and February 2022 put water through parts of town that had stayed dry for a generation. So it is worth being blunt about what a container does. It keeps rain off from above and it locks. It is not a barrier against rising water. Once the level reaches the door sill, water gets past the seals and into the box, and an empty container carries enough trapped air to lift off the ground and drift. If a seller tells you different, they are either guessing or not being straight with you. None of that makes a container a poor store in this town. It makes it one that has to be sited by somebody thinking about water rather than about how far it is from the back door, which is the decision most people get wrong.

What actually protects your gear is height and position. Pick the highest ground you can genuinely use, even if it means a longer walk from the back door with an armful of gear. Stay off the line water takes when it runs across the block, because around here a gully going hard does as much harm as the river coming up. If it has to live on low ground, we can set it up on a raised pad or on blocks so the floor sits well clear and the underside stays ventilated, and we can talk about anchoring so it does not travel if it ever gets buoyant. And think about what goes where inside it. Shelving at chest height is worth a great deal more than floor space for anything you would be upset to lose.

sections.h: When lifting beats backing in
p: A crane delivery gets treated as the expensive option, and on a Gympie ridge block it is often the cheap one, because it goes in first time. A tilt-tray needs a straight, reasonably flat run of nine or ten metres for a 20ft, and it needs the driveway to stay at roughly the same grade the whole way. Half the streets off Tozer Street and up around Victory Heights cannot offer that. A crane truck stands on the road, lifts the unit over the fence or the carport and sets it exactly where you want it, which on a narrow block is also the only way to get it hard against a boundary. What decides whether that works is reach and what is in the way: how far the container has to travel horizontally, the height of the roofline or the trees it clears, whether anything is strung overhead at the front of the property, and whether there is enough road width to get the outriggers down without closing it off. Two photos answer most of that — one from the middle of the road looking at the house, one from the spot looking back toward the street.

faqs.q: Do you actually have containers in Gympie, or do they come from Brisbane?
faqs.a: We hold stock at a depot in Gympie. Not every size and grade is standing there every week, and where we do not have what you want locally it comes up from our Cornubia yard on the next run, but a straightforward 20ft is usually available in town. You can come and look at one, though it has to be arranged first — there is no counter and nobody waiting at the gate. We do not print that address anywhere, because an unannounced visit just means a locked fence and a wasted trip.

faqs.q: My driveway drops away hard from the road at Victory Heights. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Usually, but probably not on a tilt-tray. Where the drive pitches down steeply off the kerb, the rear of the bed grounds on the bitumen before the container has cleared it, and no amount of care changes that. The usual fix is a crane truck standing on the road and lifting the unit over the fence, or dropping a size where a 40ft was the original idea. Stand at the kerb, take one picture up the drive and one looking back down it, and we can normally settle it over the phone.

faqs.q: Is a container a sensible store on a flood-prone Gympie block?
faqs.a: Yes, provided you treat it as a lock-up rather than a barrier. Once water reaches the door sill it works past the seals, and an empty unit carries enough trapped air to lift and drift. Elevation is what actually saves the contents. Choose height over convenience when you pick the spot, keep the unit off the line water takes when it runs across the block, and think about standing it on blocks or a built pad so the floor sits above the surface. Set up that way it earns its keep; bought as flood protection it will disappoint you at the worst possible moment.

faqs.q: Can you get a container down a Mary Valley property driveway?
faqs.a: Regularly, and most of them are fine when the surface is dry and bound. What stops us is a greasy formed-earth drive after rain, a table drain a wheel can drop into, a private grid nobody can put a load rating to, and no room to line up straight at the far end. Where any of that applies, the fallback is to stand the container on firm ground near the road so you can drag it in with the tractor in your own time, or to send a crane truck that can park once and reach further than a tilt could. Say so at the booking rather than at the front gate.

locations.name: Hervey Bay
locations.depot: our Gympie depot up the Bruce, with anything not standing there carted from the Cornubia yard
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray on the flat coastal blocks; crane truck for village lots, tight culs-de-sac and anything going over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Hervey Bay. Sandy ground, over-50s village access and boat and van storage handled by people who deliver here.
locations.line: Nothing about the run to Hervey Bay is hard. It is flat, it is sealed, and a truck gets from the Bruce to Urangan without meeting a hill worth mentioning. The whole job is the last thirty metres, and it is nearly always one of two things: sand that carries far less than it looks like it will, or a village or estate road built to a scale that stops at a removalist truck. Sort those two out at the quote and a Hervey Bay delivery is a quiet twenty minutes.
locations.uses: boat, tinnie and trailer storage where a double garage was never going to hold the van as well, caravan gear and annexes packed away between trips, fishing and crabbing kit for the Great Sandy Strait crowd, downsizers storing a lifetime of a Melbourne or Sydney house while a smaller place gets sorted out, trade storage for the builders working the new estates at Eli Waters, Nikenbah and Urraween, dry storage on the acreage through Dundowran, Takura and Craignish, and gear stores for the tour, charter and hire operators running out of Urangan
access: Sand is the through-line here. From Point Vernon around through Pialba, Scarness, Torquay and Urangan the profile is coastal sand over a water table that is not far down, and it behaves the same way everywhere: it drains beautifully, it carries badly, and it looks solid right up until a loaded rear axle proves it is not. A truck can sit down to the diffs on a nature strip that a car park on all winter. Behind the strip the newer estates at Eli Waters, Kawungan and Nikenbah are cut and filled, and eighteen-month-old fill under thin turf is its own kind of soft. Further out toward Booral, Dundowran Beach and Craignish it goes to sand over coffee rock in places, which is firm as concrete in one spot and hollow two metres away. None of it is a reason not to deliver. It is a reason to bring something to spread the load and to know before the truck is committed. The second constraint is the shape of the place. Hervey Bay has a lot of over-50s and lifestyle villages, and the internal roads in those are narrow, speed-humped, tightly radiused and often gated with a height bar. A rigid truck carrying six metres of container past the rear axle does not swing through a village turning circle designed for a courier van. Body corporate notice, a booked window and a manager who knows you are coming make the difference between an easy job and a truck sitting at the boom gate. The older bayside blocks at Point Vernon and Torquay bring narrow side gates, established figs and low service lines across the frontage, which usually means lifting over rather than backing in. And it is worth saying that half the district is retired and quiet on a weekday morning, so a bit of warning to the neighbours about the noise costs nothing and buys goodwill.

sections.h: Why sand needs something under the corners
p: A container puts everything it weighs, plus everything you load into it, down through four small steel castings at the corners. That is a lot of tonnage arriving on four dinner-plate-sized patches of ground. Straight onto Hervey Bay sand, or onto turf with sand under it, none of that load spreads out. It punches down, and it does not punch down evenly, because no block is uniform. What you get a season later is a unit sitting out of square, and the first thing that tells you is the doors — one starts to catch, then it takes a shoulder, then it takes two people. The frame is racked at that point and getting it back is a lift, not an adjustment.

The fix costs almost nothing and it is done at delivery. Bearers or pads set under each casting, bedded down onto something firm and checked across both diagonals, spread the load wide enough that the sand can hold it. On the coastal strip we like to get the floor a hundred millimetres or more clear of the ground as well, because the water table is shallow and a steel floor sitting hard against damp sand for a decade is where problems start from underneath rather than from the roof. It also makes the unit far easier to pick up and shift later, which matters if you ever sell the place or rearrange the yard — a unit that has bedded itself down into wet sand needs digging out before anybody can get a chain on it. Mention the ground when you enquire and the materials come on the truck with the container.

sections.h: Villages, estates and the boom gate
p: A large slice of Hervey Bay lives behind a gate, and delivering into a lifestyle village or a body corporate estate is a scheduling problem more than a driving one. The pattern is consistent: management wants notice and a nominated time, they will want the transport operator to hold insurance, and they may have a preferred route through the site that avoids the narrow section past the clubhouse. Internal roads are built to a domestic scale, so speed humps, tight corner radii and a turning circle at the end of a cul-de-sac that suits a garbage truck and nothing longer all come into it. Height bars on the entry are common and they are not negotiable on the day, and a boom gate that has been set for visitor parking will not simply lift for a truck because it has arrived.

None of that is difficult, but it has to happen a week out rather than on the morning. Get the approval in hand, get a window, then let us build a run around it. Where the internal roads genuinely will not take a truck with a container behind the cab, the workable answer is often a crane truck standing outside the boundary and lifting in, or a smaller unit than you first had in mind. A 10ft on a village lot does more than people expect and it goes places a 20ft cannot, and on a courtyard site it is frequently the only size that leaves you room to open the doors afterwards. Tell us at the enquiry that it is a village or estate address and we will ask the right questions rather than finding out at the gate.

sections.h: Hire when the need has an end date
p: A lot of what we do here runs on a calendar. Somebody sells up down south, arrives with a full container of furniture and needs it somewhere secure for four months while a build finishes. A charter or hire operator wants gear locked away between the whale season and the next one. A builder needs somewhere lockable on a job at Kawungan for as long as the program runs and not one day past handover. Hire fits all of those, because nobody wants to be advertising a second-hand container in June, and the truck at the far end is our problem rather than yours. If the job changes shape halfway through, a hire unit can be traded for a different size, which is not an option once you own one.

Buying starts to win the moment nobody can say when the need finishes, or where the unit turns into part of the furniture — a permanent store on an acreage block at Takura, a lock-up on a leased yard. If it is going to sit outdoors in salt air all year with anything in it you want kept dry, ask us for cargo-worthy, which is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. The grades page sets out what the differences actually are, and it is worth two minutes before you decide on price alone. The other thing worth weighing is what happens at the end. A bought 20ft in reasonable condition holds its value in this district, and there is a genuine second-hand market on the Fraser Coast when you are finished with it, which takes some of the sting out of the decision either way.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into sandy ground at Torquay or Urangan?
faqs.a: Not evenly, which is the problem. Sand and thin turf cannot spread the load that four corner castings put into them, so one corner goes down further than the others and the doors start telling you about it within a season or two. Bearers or pads underneath each casting, bedded down and checked across both diagonals, deal with it for good and lift the floor clear of a shallow water table at the same time. Describe the ground when you ring and the materials come out on the truck with the container.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into an over-50s village or gated estate in Hervey Bay?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens often, but it needs organising rather than just booking. Management will generally want written notice, a nominated delivery window and evidence of insurance from the transport operator, and there may be a height bar at the entry or a route through the site that avoids the tightest corners. Sort the approval and the window out first, then ring us with it. Where the internal roads will not take a truck with a container on the back, a crane lift from outside the boundary or a smaller unit usually solves it.

faqs.q: Can you get a container across to K'gari?
faqs.a: That last leg goes on a barge, and what a barge will carry — length, weight, how it loads and when it runs — is the operator's call, not ours. We sort that out with them while we are pricing your job, so you end up with a single figure rather than a container price and a vague wave toward the water. We deliberately keep timetables off this page, because those arrangements move and a stale web page costs you a morning standing at a ramp. A 20ft travels and places far more easily over there than a 40ft.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Hervey Bay take?
faqs.a: Three to five business days is the usual window from order. A plain 20ft heading to a block with an easy approach sits at the short end of that. It stretches out where a crane has to be booked, where we are waiting on a village delivery window, or where the grade or configuration you have asked for has to come up from our Cornubia yard. Where the date is locked in at your end — a handover, a truck full of furniture arriving, a season about to start — tell us when you ring and the run gets planned to suit it.

locations.name: Maryborough
locations.depot: our Gympie depot, an easy run north up the Bruce, backed by the Cornubia yard
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for most of the old grid; crane truck for 40ft and for high-set houses where the only usable ground is out the back
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Maryborough. Wide heritage streets, high-set Queenslanders and Mary River flats — access and siting sorted first.
locations.line: Maryborough is the easiest town on this stretch of coast to get a truck around, and it is not close. The surveyors laid out a proper grid with generous carriageways when the port was the point of the place, and a century and a half on, that grid still swallows a rigid truck without complaint. What it does not solve is the two things that are actually particular to Maryborough: houses built high off the ground on stumps with the good yard underneath them, and a river that has come up over Tinana and Granville often enough for everyone to have an opinion about levels.
locations.uses: workshop and machinery storage for the rail, engineering and fabrication trades around the Maryborough industrial area, cane gear and irrigation fittings on the river flats out through Tinana, Owanyilla and Yengarie, timber, tools and salvaged joinery for the people restoring the old timber houses in the character streets, feed and fencing on the smaller holdings toward Tiaro, Bauple and Aldershot, stock and equipment storage for the businesses along Adelaide and Kent Streets that have run out of room upstairs, and household storage while a high-set is restumped
access: Start with the good news, because Maryborough deserves it. The old town grid — Kent, Adelaide, Bazaar, Ellena, Alice and the streets around them — has wide carriageways, generous corner radii and long straight runs, which means a tilt-tray with a 20ft on it can position properly instead of doing a three-point turn against a kerb. Very few regional towns give you that. The catch is what happens once the truck stops. Maryborough housing is high-set timber on stumps, and on a lot of blocks the only space worth putting a container is either right underneath the house, which it will not fit under, or out the back past a side gate the builder sized for a wheelbarrow in 1912. Add a mature mango, a poinciana or a camphor laurel with limbs down at three and a half metres and a lifted tilt bed has nowhere to go. On those blocks a crane truck standing in the street and lifting over the house is not exotic, it is just the way it is done. The other half of the district is the flats. Tinana, Granville, Baddow, Aldershot and the low country along the Mary and Tinana Creek sit on alluvial silt and heavy river soil. That ground carries a truck fine through the dry months and turns to something else entirely after a wet week, and it holds water long after the surface has crusted over. Cane country out toward Owanyilla and Yengarie brings farm tracks, headland turns that are tighter than they look from the road, and irrigation mains under crossings that are not built for twenty tonne stopped on top of them. If your address is on the flats, tell us what the last stretch is and when it last rained, and if it is in the old town, tell us about the side gate and the trees rather than the street. The street is almost never the problem here.

sections.h: High-set houses and the side gate problem
p: The single most common Maryborough conversation is about a block where the street is wide, the driveway is fine and the container still cannot get to where you want it. Timber houses on stumps take up the middle of the lot, the side setback is narrow, and whatever gate exists was cut for a person and a mower. A tilt-tray needs to reverse into a straight run and slide the unit off along the ground, and it needs that run to be clear the whole way, not clear for the first four metres. Once there is a house corner, a tank stand or a stump line in the way, that is the end of it. It is worth measuring the narrowest point of the side access before you order rather than eyeing it off, because the tilt bed is wider than the container and gateposts on these old blocks have usually been clipped once already.

So we lift instead. A crane truck sets up on the road, picks the container up and puts it down in the back yard over the house or the fence. Everything that decides whether it works can be measured: the horizontal distance from wherever the truck can legally stand, the height of the ridgeline or the trees it must clear, anything strung overhead at the front of the property, and whether the carriageway leaves room for outriggers. Maryborough streets generally do give that room, which is precisely why crane work here is more straightforward than it is in most towns of this size. Three photographs answer nearly all of it: one from the footpath looking at the house, one taken from where you want the container standing looking back toward the road, and one looking straight up at whatever crosses your frontage.

sections.h: The flats, the river and honest expectations
p: Tinana, Granville, Baddow and the low ground along the river have been under water more than once in living memory, and anyone buying a container to store things on that country should hear the same thing we tell everyone. A container is an excellent lock-up and it keeps rain out from above. It is not a flood barrier. Once the level touches the door sill it finds its way past the seals, and an empty steel box with air trapped in it lifts and travels once the water gets deep enough. That is not a reason to avoid one. It is a reason to put it in the right place, and to think about what sits on the floor of it versus what sits on a shelf at chest height, because that single decision is what most people wish they had made differently afterwards.

The right place is high. Take the best ground you have, keep off the route water travels when it crosses the block, and where there is no high ground to be had, stand the unit on blocks or a built pad so the floor sits above the surface with air moving under it. On the flats there is a second reason to do that anyway, which is that heavy river soil holds moisture for weeks and a floor bearing on damp ground for years does not thank you for it. If the container is going to live down there long-term, talk to us about anchoring as well, so it stays put rather than travelling if it ever gets buoyant. A unit that moves in a flood stops being your problem alone the moment it ends up against somebody else's fence.

sections.h: Character streets and what the neighbours see
p: Maryborough takes its heritage seriously and large parts of the old town sit inside character and heritage precincts. That does not usually stop a container going onto a block, but it does change where it can sensibly sit and how visible it should be, and there are situations — anything permanent, anything altering a listed building, anything prominent from a street with a heritage character — where the council position is worth checking before you order rather than after. We are not going to guess at the rule for your particular lot, because it varies, it changes, and it is yours to confirm rather than ours to promise. What we can tell you is that the question comes up often enough here to be worth a phone call to council at the planning stage, and that the people on the counter deal with it regularly and are not difficult about it.

The practical guidance is the same as it is anywhere, just applied a bit more carefully here. Set back from the road, softened by a fence or a bit of planting, and not the first thing anybody notices walking past will keep the neighbours and the council equally relaxed. Sitting on the front lawn of a Queenslander in one of the character streets will not. And where you intend to clad it, paint it something that vanishes into the yard, or hang a lean-to off one side, decide that before delivery rather than after, because the finish is far easier to apply with clear space on all four sides. Moving a container twenty metres once the truck has gone is a second delivery, not a tweak, and it is charged like one.

faqs.q: My house at Maryborough is high-set with a narrow side gate. Can a container get to the back yard?
faqs.a: Not on a tilt-tray, most likely, but yes with a crane truck. It stands in the street, picks the container up over the house or the side fence and sets it down where you want it. Maryborough streets are wide enough to get outriggers out properly, which makes this easier here than in most towns of the size. Tell us how far it is from the road to the spot, how high the roof or the trees in between are, and whether anything is strung overhead at the front. Two photos, one from the footpath and one from the back yard, will usually settle it.

faqs.q: How long does a container take to reach Maryborough?
faqs.a: Three to five business days is normal. It is quicker where a standard 20ft is already standing at our Gympie depot and the approach at your end is clear, and it stretches where a crane has to be booked, where you have asked for a specific grade or configuration that has to come from Cornubia, or where wet weather has put a river-flat address out of action for a couple of days. If there is a fixed date on your end, tell us when you enquire.

faqs.q: Can I put a container on a block at Tinana or Granville that has flooded before?
faqs.a: You can, and plenty do, but choose the spot for elevation rather than for how close it is to the house. A container will not hold water out — once the level touches the door sill it gets past the seals, and an empty one lifts and travels once it is deep enough. Take the best ground on the block, keep off the route water takes when it crosses, and where the whole lot is low, stand it on blocks or a built pad so the floor sits clear. For anything living down there permanently, anchoring is worth talking through.

faqs.q: Do I need approval for a container in a Maryborough heritage or character street?
faqs.a: That turns on how long it is staying, how obvious it is from the footpath, and whether your property or the precinct around it carries a listing — and we are not going to guess at your particular lot. Ring council at the planning stage rather than after the truck has been. As a rule of thumb, short-term and screened almost never causes trouble, while permanent, prominent or modified is where somebody starts asking questions. Answering it early is much cheaper than paying for a second delivery to shift the thing.

locations.name: Bundaberg
locations.depot: our Gympie depot or the Cornubia yard, depending on which has the size and grade you are after
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–6 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft; crane truck for 40ft, and a longer trailer for farm drops with a straight run in
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Bundaberg. Red soil, cane tramway crossings and salt air at Bargara, planned for how the district works.
locations.line: Two things shape a Bundaberg delivery and neither is the highway. The first is red soil, which is superb country to grow things in and a genuinely deceptive surface to park twenty tonne on — it sets like a road in October and turns greasy within an hour of a storm. The second is that a lot of the district is cut up by cane tramway, and from about June the roads and headlands are busy with bins and haul-outs that were there first. Work around both and the run is easy.
locations.uses: chemical, fertiliser and irrigation fittings kept locked and dry on the cane and small crop farms out through Bundaberg North, Gooburrum and Bucca, packing shed overflow for the macadamia, avocado and sweet potato growers around Childers and Wallaville, seasonal storage for the labour and harvest contractors who need gear to disappear between crops, boat, dive and fishing gear on the coastal strip at Bargara, Innes Park and Elliott Heads, site stores on the builds through Avoca, Kalkie and Ashfield, and secure storage for the marine and workshop trades near Burnett Heads
access: Red basaltic soil is the signature of this district and it deserves respect. Dry, it is hard, well graded and carries a loaded truck as well as a formed road. Wet, it is slick on top with grip underneath, which is a worse combination than plain mud because the wheels break away before the driver has any warning. It also stains everything it touches, which matters less to a container than it does to a paved driveway a truck has just tracked across. Out on the farms, the working surfaces are headlands and farm tracks, and headlands are built for a tractor turning circle rather than a rigid truck with six metres hanging past the rear axle. Cane tramway crossings are everywhere across this country and they are worth flagging when you book — a private crossing is not always sitting at the same level as the road either side, and a long truck can hang up on the hump if the approach is short. From the middle of the year the tramways and the haul roads are working, and a delivery that ignores the harvest is a delivery that spends an hour waiting for a train of bins. Closer to town, Bundaberg North, Kepnock, Kalkie and Avoca are ordinary suburban work with the usual mix of narrow older frontages and cut-and-fill estate blocks where the ground has not settled. The coastal strip is different again. Bargara, Innes Park, Coral Cove and Elliott Heads sit on sand and coral rubble with salt in the air off the water, so the ground carries poorly and anything steel that sits there permanently needs a bit more thought about how it is set up and how it is kept. And the low country along the Burnett — North Bundaberg in particular — has a history that anyone siting a long-term store down there ought to factor in before they choose the spot.

sections.h: Red soil, and what to put under the corners
p: The reason we keep going on about what a container sits on is that this district makes it matter more than most. Red volcanic soil is deep, it holds water, and it moves through the year — swelling through the wet and shrinking back through the dry, and never evenly across a block. A container dropped straight onto red soil goes along for the ride, corner by corner, and the moment those four load points stop sitting level with each other the frame is trying to carry itself on three of them. The visible symptom is always the doors: one starts to bind, then it needs a shove, then it needs two people and a bar. By then the frame is racked and the fix is a lift and a reset, not a shim.

Prevention is a few pads or bearers under the castings, bedded onto something that will not sink and checked across both diagonals before the truck leaves. Face the doors uphill wherever the ground falls, so they swing with gravity instead of fighting it, and leave clear air underneath so water drains off and the underside can breathe. On red soil we also like to keep the grass down around the bottom rail, because vegetation held against steel traps moisture for months at a time and that is what starts the corrosion, not the weather itself. Ten minutes with a whipper snipper twice a year decides whether the bottom rail is still clean steel in twenty years or a line of scale you are grinding back.

sections.h: Farms, harvest and getting the timing right
p: A farm delivery in this district is usually easy and occasionally impossible, and the difference is almost always the last three hundred metres rather than the property itself. Headland turns are sized for machinery that pivots, not for a rigid truck that needs to swing wide and then straighten. Private tramway crossings can sit proud of the road, which will hang up a long truck with a short approach. Irrigation mains and drainage pipes run under farm crossings that were built for a tractor and a bin, not for twenty tonne standing still on top of them. And from the middle of the year through to about the end of the season, the tramway and the haul roads are in use.

None of that is a problem if we know about it. Tell us when you book what the approach is, whether there is a crossing on it, and whether harvest traffic is running. Where the track will not carry a loaded truck, the standard answer in this district is to stand the container on the hardstand by the shed or up near the road and let you drag it into position with the tractor when it suits. That is often cleaner than threading a truck down a track that will need grading afterwards, and it puts the timing back in your hands rather than ours. Where the shed itself is the destination and the approach is genuinely tight, a crane truck standing on firm ground and reaching in will usually get further than a tilt-tray that has to drive the whole way.

sections.h: The coastal strip is a different job
p: Twenty minutes east of the city and everything changes. Bargara, Burnett Heads, Innes Park, Coral Cove and Elliott Heads sit on sand and coral rubble with salt in the air off the water, and both of those affect a container over the long term. Sand carries badly, so bearers or pads under the corners are not optional if you want the unit to still be square in five years. Salt air is not the killer people assume — these things spent their working lives crossing oceans — but a container sitting still under a casuarina with wet leaf litter on the roof and long grass against the bottom rail is in a completely different situation to one on a ship. That is where corrosion actually starts.

The maintenance list is short and it is the whole list. Sweep the roof a couple of times a year so leaf litter is not sitting on a panel holding water. Keep the grass down around the base. Leave a gap underneath so air moves. Open the doors on a dry day now and then to clear any condensation. Do that on the coast here and a unit that would otherwise look tired quickly stays sound for decades. If it is going to live out there permanently with anything you need to stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy, which is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard, and have a look at the grades page before you make the call on price alone.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a cane farm out past Gooburrum or Bucca?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a big part of what goes to this district. What we need to know is what the last few hundred metres looks like: whether there is a tramway crossing on the approach and how it sits relative to the road, whether the headland has a real turning area or just a tractor-sized one, and whether harvest traffic is running. Where the track will not carry a loaded truck, we stand the container on firm ground by the shed or up near the road and you drag it into place with the tractor when it suits. Raise it at the booking rather than at the gate.

faqs.q: What does red soil do to a container over time?
faqs.a: It moves under it. Red volcanic soil takes up water through the wet and shrinks back through the dry, unevenly across a block, and a container placed straight onto it follows that movement one corner at a time. Once the four corner castings are at different heights the frame racks and the doors stop closing properly. Pads or bearers under each casting, bedded firm and checked across both diagonals, head all of it off for very little money. Our drivers do that setup at delivery wherever the site lets them — just describe the ground when you ring.

faqs.q: How quickly can you get a container to Bundaberg?
faqs.a: Three to six business days is the normal window from order. A standard 20ft going to a clear address at the shorter end, and it stretches where a crane is needed, where a specific grade or configuration has to come from Cornubia rather than Gympie, or where rain has taken a farm track or a soft block off the list for a couple of days. Where your date is fixed, say so when you ring and the run gets planned to suit it rather than the reverse.

faqs.q: Should I be worried about salt air at Bargara or Innes Park?
faqs.a: Less than most people expect, and more about the things around it than the sea breeze. What actually starts corrosion is wet leaf litter sitting on the roof, grass and vegetation trapping moisture against the bottom rail, and a floor bearing directly on damp sand for years. Get it up on pads with air moving underneath, sweep the roof occasionally, keep the base clear, and it will hold up for decades. For anything permanent on the coastal strip that has to stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy — it is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard.

locations.line: Gladstone runs on projects, and projects run on dates. A shutdown has a start and a finish written on a wall somewhere, and everything feeding it either lands inside that window or is a problem. That is the main thing we plan around here — not the drive, which is straightforward, but the gate. The other half of the district is domestic, and Gladstone housing is built across some genuinely steep ground with cut-and-fill blocks and retaining walls that decide where a container can go long before you do.
locations.uses: laydown and consumables storage on the industrial sites through Yarwun, Targinie and the Callemondah corridor, tool and spares stores for the contractors working shutdowns and maintenance campaigns, secure storage for the trades based out of the Clinton and Aerodrome Road industrial area, boat, crab pot and camping gear at Tannum Sands, Boyne Island and Benaraby, site stores on the builds around Kirkwood, New Auckland and Glen Eden, and feed, fencing and machinery storage on the grazing country out toward Calliope, Mount Larcom and Ubobo
access: There are two Gladstones for a delivery driver and they have almost nothing in common. The industrial side is technically easy and administratively particular. Hardstand, wide gates, room to swing, a forklift or a crane usually already on site — but also inductions, gate passes, escorts, permits to work, high-visibility and boot requirements, and nominated delivery windows that are enforced rather than suggested. A truck without paperwork does not get through the boom, and that is nobody's fault but it is everybody's delay. Sort the site requirements out with your contractor or the site coordinator first, tell us what the driver needs to carry and what time the window is, and the job runs like clockwork. The domestic side is where the driving gets interesting. Gladstone is built over hills and the residential suburbs — West Gladstone, Kin Kora, Sun Valley, Barney Point, Telina, Clinton — are full of blocks that have been cut into or filled out from a slope, with retaining walls, short steep driveways and level changes between the street and the yard. A driveway that turns and rises at the same time is the one that gets a tilt-tray. The bed grounds out on the transition, or the truck cannot straighten before it runs out of driveway. On plenty of those a crane lift from the street is the only sensible method, and the constraint becomes reach across a retaining wall and the height of anything in between. Out at Tannum Sands, Boyne Island and the coastal edge you swap hills for sand and salt air. Further inland toward Calliope, Mount Larcom and the grazing country it is rural: unsealed approaches, grids of unknown rating, creek crossings that come up fast in the wet, and turning space at the shed that needs to be actual rather than assumed.

sections.h: Getting a truck through the gate
p: Industrial delivery in Gladstone is not hard, it is procedural, and the failures are almost always paperwork rather than access. Every major site here runs its own induction, its own permit system and its own delivery scheduling, and the requirements are not identical between them. The transport operator generally needs a nominated arrival window, a contact who will actually meet the truck, evidence of insurance, and whatever the site demands of a driver in terms of induction and personal protective equipment. Some sites want a vehicle inspection at the gate. Some want an escort from the boom to the laydown area. None of it is unreasonable and none of it is negotiable at seven in the morning with a loaded truck idling at the entry, which is where these things get discovered when nobody has asked in advance.

What we ask for at the booking is simple: the site, the gate you want the truck to use, the window you have been given, the name and number of the person meeting it, and any induction or documentation the driver has to have. Give us that and the container lands in the right place at the right hour. Leave it vague and the truck sits at a boom gate burning your window and ours. If your delivery is tied to a shutdown that has a hard start, say so early and we will build backwards from that date rather than forwards from the order, because a container that lands the day after the crews arrive has already failed at the only thing it was there to do. The same goes for demobilisation — tell us the finish date at the start and the pick-up gets scheduled with everything else rather than becoming a phone call you make in a hurry.

sections.h: Hire that matches a campaign
p: Shutdown and project work is exactly the situation hire was invented for. You need secure, weatherproof storage on a laydown for six or ten or fourteen weeks, you need it on site before the crews arrive, and you need it gone once demobilisation is finished. Owning the asset for that is the wrong shape — you carry it on the books, you store it between campaigns, and you organise the trucking at both ends. Hire puts a date on it, gets it off site when the job is done, and lets you scale the number up or down as the scope changes, which on a campaign it invariably does. It also keeps the cost sitting against the job rather than against the balance sheet, which is usually where a project manager wants it.

Buying makes better sense where the container becomes permanent infrastructure — a consumables store on a yard you lease at Clinton, a spares lock-up you will still have in five years, a store on a grazing property out at Calliope. It also makes sense where you want to modify it, because a hire unit comes back the way it went out. If it is going to live outdoors on an industrial site holding anything you need to stay dry, ask for cargo-worthy, which is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard. Tell us the duration and what is going inside and we will tell you which way round it should be, including the case where the answer is one bought unit for the permanent store and two hired ones over the top of a campaign. That combination is common here and it is usually the cheapest way through.

sections.h: Cut, fill and where it can actually land
p: Gladstone housing is built across slopes, and a great many blocks have been made level by cutting into the hill on one side and filling out on the other. That has two consequences worth thinking about before you order. The first is that the flat part of your yard may be fill, and fill that has not been through many wet seasons behaves quite differently from the cut side. The second is that retaining walls are structural and they have a design load that did not contemplate a container sitting against them or a truck standing on the fill behind them. Setting a six-metre steel box hard up against the top of a retaining wall is a conversation with an engineer, not a delivery decision.

In practice we look for the firmest, most level, least loaded part of the block, which is often not the spot the customer had in mind. Getting the unit onto the cut side or onto an existing slab or driveway apron is worth losing a few metres of convenience for. Where the fall across the block is significant, we build the low side up with pads or bearers instead of digging the high side out, because cutting into a slope only carves a trench for water to sit in alongside the unit. Get the door end onto the high side of the fall while you are at it, so the doors swing with gravity rather than against it. That distinction gets missed constantly and it is the difference between a store you open with one hand for twenty years and one that needs a shoulder by the second winter.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container onto a Gladstone industrial site with induction requirements?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is routine, but the paperwork has to be sorted before the day. Tell us at the booking which site and which gate, the delivery window you have been given, who is meeting the truck, and exactly what the driver needs to hold in the way of induction, insurance evidence and protective equipment. Some sites require an escort from the boom to the laydown. Give us all of that up front and the job runs to time. Leave it until the morning and the truck sits at the gate.

faqs.q: Can I hire containers just for the length of a shutdown?
faqs.a: That is one of the main reasons hire exists here. You set a start and a finish, we get the units on the laydown before the crews arrive and off site once demobilisation is done, and you are not carrying an asset or organising storage between campaigns. If the scope changes mid-campaign, the number of units can change with it. Tell us the dates, the site access requirements and roughly what is going inside, and we will quote the whole thing including getting them there and away again.

faqs.q: My block at Kin Kora is on a slope with a retaining wall. Where can the container go?
faqs.a: Usually somewhere, but probably not where you first pictured. Retaining walls have a design load and a container plus contents sitting on the fill behind one is not something to decide on the day — that is an engineering question. We look for the firmest and most level part of the block, which is often the cut side, an existing slab or the driveway apron. Where there is a fall, we build the low side up with pads or bearers rather than cutting the high side away, which only makes a channel for water to pond against the unit.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Gladstone take?
faqs.a: Four to seven business days is the usual window, and site deliveries are scheduled around your induction and gate access rather than around our run, so a firm window at your end tightens ours. It stretches where a crane truck is needed, where a particular grade or size has to come north, or where wet weather has made a rural approach out toward Calliope or Ubobo unsafe for a loaded truck. If the date is tied to a shutdown start, tell us early and we will plan backwards from it.

locations.line: There is stock in Rockhampton, which is the single most useful fact on this page, because it means a container for a Rockhampton address does not have to be trucked a thousand kilometres before it does any work. The thing that catches people out here is not supply and it is not the highway. It is black soil. Heavy cracking clay opens up wide enough in October to lose a tape measure down, closes over in the wet, and will quietly take one corner of a container with it if nobody put anything underneath.
locations.uses: feed, vet supplies, fencing and panels on the grazing country through Gracemere, Stanwell, Bajool and out west toward Duaringa, spares and consumables for the mining services and engineering firms that supply the Bowen Basin, tool and plant storage on the industrial land at Parkhurst and Gracemere, boat, camping and fishing gear at Yeppoon and Emu Park where the shed filled up long ago, secure site stores for the builders working Norman Gardens and Parkhurst, and stock overflow for businesses that have outgrown a leased tenancy
access: Black soil is the local specialist subject and every long-term container in this district lives or dies by how it was dealt with. Cracking clay on the Fitzroy country shrinks hard through the dry and swells through the wet, and it does not do either uniformly. A truck crossing it in October has a firm, cracked, roadlike surface. The same paddock a fortnight into a wet is a surface that will not hold a wheel, and a loaded rigid that leaves the formed track on black soil after rain is not getting itself out. Around town, the ground splits along the same lines as the flood history. Depot Hill, Port Curtis, Allenstown and the low ground near the river are alluvial and flat. The Range, Frenchville, Norman Gardens and Kawana sit higher, on better-draining country with more slope and more rock, and the driveways up there are the ones that need looking at before a tilt-tray is committed. The city grid itself is generous, laid out wide when Rockhampton was a river port, which means a truck can position properly in most streets. Out west and out to the coast, the pattern changes again. The properties toward Gracemere, Stanwell, Bajool and Duaringa are grid-and-gate rural: private grids nobody can rate, cattle on the road, long formed-earth drives, and turning space at the shed. The Capricorn Coast run to Yeppoon and Emu Park swaps that for sand and salt. And then there is heat, which is a genuine access issue here rather than a comfort one — a black steel box standing in a Rockhampton yard through a summer afternoon reaches temperatures that decide what you can sensibly keep in it and whether the unit needs venting. That is a question worth answering at the quote, not after the first February.

sections.h: Local stock, and the corridor west
p: We hold containers at a depot in Rockhampton. That matters for two reasons. The obvious one is speed — a unit already standing in town can be on a Rockhampton, Gracemere or Yeppoon address in a day or two rather than waiting on a truck coming north. The less obvious one is that it makes the whole region workable. Rockhampton is the front door for a lot of country that has no realistic container supply of its own, and having stock here is what makes a delivery out to the grazing country or west along the Capricorn Highway a run rather than an expedition. It also means we can be flexible when something changes. A booking pulled because a paddock has gone soft, or a unit that needs to come back and be swapped, is a short trip rather than a thousand-kilometre problem, and that is what decides whether a supplier is any use to you when a job does not go to plan.

Looking at a unit before you order is welcome and it needs arranging, since there is no public counter at the depot. Ring, tell us what you are after, and we will lock in a time with somebody on hand and the unit pulled out where you can open the doors and walk the length of the floor. If the trip does not suit, photos of the actual unit are available on request and we send them before delivery, covering the roof, both ends, the corner posts and the full length of the floor. And be specific at the enquiry about what you want, because what is standing locally changes week to week, and if a particular size or grade has to come up from Cornubia you should hear that when you ask rather than when you are waiting.

sections.h: Black soil will move your container if you let it
p: This is the one thing worth reading twice if the container is going onto clay. A shipping container carries its whole weight, plus everything you put in it, through the four castings at its corners. It is designed that way and it is fine, provided those four points stay at the same height relative to each other. Cracking clay makes no such promise. It heaves through the wet and shrinks through the dry, unevenly, and over two or three seasons it will lift one corner and drop another. Once that happens the frame is racked, and a racked container is one whose doors stop lining up. First one catches. Then it needs a bar. Then it needs a lift and a reset, which costs a great deal more than doing it right at the start.

What works out here is spreading the load onto something that will not follow the soil. Concrete pads, heavy hardwood bearers, or a pair of sleepers under each end, bedded down into firm ground and checked level across both diagonals before the truck leaves. Have the doors facing uphill wherever there is a fall. Leave a gap beneath so water drains away and air circulates instead of sitting up against the floor. And if the container is going on genuinely reactive country and it is staying for the long haul, it is worth putting it on a small prepared pad of compacted road base — an hour with a bobcat before delivery is cheaper than any of the alternatives afterwards.

sections.h: Heat, ventilation and what you keep inside
p: Rockhampton summers do things to a sealed steel box that people from further south do not always anticipate. A closed container standing in the sun gets hot, and then it stays hot well into the evening because the mass takes a long time to give it back. That is irrelevant if you are storing steel, fencing gear, panels or tools. It is very relevant if you are storing anything with a temperature range on the label — chemicals, adhesives, paint, batteries, electronics, sealed food, timber you care about, or anything with a rubber or plastic component that will go off early. Humidity plays into it as well, because a box that heats hard during the day and cools overnight will move moisture around inside itself, and that condensation has to land somewhere. On a sealed unit with no ventilation, it lands on the ceiling and drips.

There are sensible answers and they are worth deciding on before delivery rather than after. Vents fitted high and low get air moving through and take the top off the peak. A whirlybird does more. Insulation and lining is a bigger job but turns the unit into something you can work in rather than just store in. Even orientation helps — a container placed with the long side facing the afternoon sun rather than the door end has a different day to one that catches it square. Say what is going in it and how long for, and we will point at whichever of those actually earns its money rather than reading you the catalogue. For most people out here the honest answer is a pair of vents and some thought about which way the doors face, and that is where it ends.

faqs.q: Do you keep containers in Rockhampton or do they come from down south?
faqs.a: We hold stock at a depot in Rockhampton, so a lot of local orders go out on a unit already in town. Not every size and grade is standing there in any given week — where we do not have what you want locally it comes up from the Cornubia yard and adds a few days, and you will be told which of those it is at the quote. Come and look at one by all means, but book it in first — there is nobody on the gate to let you through unannounced.

faqs.q: What should a container sit on in black soil country?
faqs.a: Not the soil. Cracking clay swells through the wet and shrinks through the dry, unevenly, and over a couple of seasons it will lift one corner casting and drop another until the frame racks and the doors stop closing. Spread the load onto something that does not follow the ground: concrete pads, heavy hardwood bearers or sleepers under each end, bedded into firm ground and levelled across both diagonals. On genuinely reactive country that is keeping a container long-term, a small prepared pad of compacted road base is worth the hour it takes.

faqs.q: Will a container be too hot to store things in through a Rockhampton summer?
faqs.a: For fencing gear, steel, panels and tools, no — it makes no practical difference. For anything with a temperature limit on the label, or anything with rubber, plastic or adhesive in it, yes, a closed steel box standing in the sun here will get hotter than you expect and stay hot into the evening. Vents fitted high and low, a whirlybird, or lining and insulating for a working space are all options. Tell us what is going inside at the enquiry and we will suggest what genuinely helps rather than the full catalogue.

faqs.q: Is a container a good store on low ground near the Fitzroy?
faqs.a: As a lock-up, yes. As protection from the river, no, and nobody should sell it to you that way. Water that reaches the door sill works past the seals, and an empty box holds enough trapped air to lift and move. On Depot Hill, Port Curtis or anywhere on the low country, take the highest ground you can use, stay off the route water travels across the block, and stand the unit on blocks or a built pad so the floor sits clear. If it is staying down there permanently, talk to us about anchoring it.

locations.line: Mackay is the one town on this coast where three completely different customers ring in the same morning. A cane grower wants somewhere lockable for chemical before the season. A mining services outfit wants six units on a yard at Paget before a shutdown starts at Moranbah. A bloke at Blacks Beach wants his boat gear out of the weather. What ties them together is the calendar, because between the crush, the Bowen Basin schedule and the wet, there is not a lot of the year in Mackay that is not somebody's busy period.

access: Cane country dictates a lot of the driving here. The Pioneer Valley and the flats out through Marian, Mirani, Walkerston and Farleigh are laced with tramway, and a private crossing is not always at the same level as the road either side, which will hang a long truck up on the hump if the approach is short. Headlands are the working roads on a cane farm and they are built around what a tractor can turn, not around a rigid truck with six metres past the rear axle. During the crush the haul roads and the tramways are busy and a delivery that ignores that spends a lot of its window waiting. Ground on the flats is heavy alluvial river soil that carries well in the dry and holds water for a long time after it stops raining, and Mackay does not do gentle rain. In a wet season the district can take more in three days than a lot of Queensland gets in a year, and a farm track that was fine on Monday is not a proposition on Thursday. The industrial side at Paget is the easy end — hardstand, wide entries, room to swing, and usually a forklift already there — with the only real constraints being yard inductions and delivery windows on the bigger tenancies. The northern beaches are sand: Bucasia, Eimeo, Shoal Point and Blacks Beach all sit on coastal profile with salt in the air, so the ground carries poorly and setup matters more. Around town the older suburbs of West Mackay, North Mackay and East Mackay have narrower frontages, established figs and mangoes at truck height and short driveways, while the newer estates at Rural View and Ooralea bring the standard estate pattern of narrow streets, cars both sides, service pits on the kerb line and fill that has not settled. And through summer, everything gets planned with one eye on the forecast.

sections.h: Stock in Mackay and the run to the Basin
p: We hold containers at a depot in Mackay. That is the difference between a container being a same-week decision and a fortnight-long logistics exercise, and it matters more the further north you go. It also makes Mackay the practical supply point for a lot of country that has nothing of its own — the Pioneer Valley, the coast toward Sarina, and the corridor west toward the Bowen Basin mining towns where a lot of the gear and consumables that go underground are staged out of a yard at Paget first. The practical effect is that a Mackay order behaves like an ordinary purchase with a date on it, rather than a freight exercise where nobody can tell you when the truck is coming. That is not a small thing this far up the coast, and it is worth asking any supplier quoting you here whether the container they are describing is actually in town.

Seeing a unit before you order one is fine by us, it just has to be booked, because the depot runs without anybody stationed on a gate for visitors. Ring, say what you are after and when suits, and we will have someone there with the unit accessible so you can open the doors and look down the floor yourself. If getting there is not practical, photos of the actual unit are available on request and we send them before delivery. What is standing in Mackay changes week to week, so if you want something particular — a high cube, a double-door unit, a specific grade — ask at the enquiry and you will get a straight answer about whether it is here or coming.

sections.h: Cyclone season, tie-downs and honest limits
p: An empty shipping container is a large object with a lot of side area and not much mass, and in a serious blow that is not a good combination. Loaded, it is a very different proposition, and most containers in this district spend their lives with enough in them that the question does not come up. But if you are putting an empty or lightly loaded unit somewhere exposed and leaving it through summer, it needs to be held down, and the way to do that depends on what it is sitting on. Bolting to a slab, cyclone-rated ground anchors with turnbuckles to the corner castings, or a set of footings poured under it are all standard approaches. Where the anchoring has to be certified — anything on a commercial site, anything a builder or an insurer is going to ask about — that is an engineer's call and it should be, because the loads involved are real numbers and not a rule of thumb.

What we will not do is tell you a container is cyclone-rated on its own. It is a well-built steel box and it will handle a great deal, but its performance in a wind event is a function of how it is anchored and how it is loaded, not of the box alone. Tell us at the quote whether it is going somewhere exposed, whether it will be sitting empty for stretches, and whether anything needs certifying, and we will set it up in a way that suits rather than leaving you to work it out in November. The other half of it is what is around the unit. Loose sheeting, stacked pallets and an unsecured awning built off the side of a container do more damage in a blow than the container ever will, and they are the things worth walking around and looking at before the season starts.

sections.h: Wet season, and planning around it
p: The wet is not a nuisance in Mackay, it is a season with a name, and it changes how a delivery is scheduled rather than whether it happens. Heavy alluvial river soil across the valley and the flats carries a loaded truck comfortably when it is dry and becomes something no amount of skill gets a rigid out of once it has had a real event on it. We would far rather ring you and shift a booking by two or three days than put a truck onto a farm track or a soft block and turn a twenty-minute job into a tractor recovery and a trench across your headland. Nobody comes out ahead from that. You are standing there watching your access get chewed up and wondering who is paying for the repair, and we have a truck and a driver tied up for the rest of the day.

So through summer we leave a bit of room in out-of-town bookings and we ring you with what is happening, instead of leaving you standing at the shed all morning for a truck that was never going to make the last kilometre. Your local knowledge is worth a lot in that conversation — you know which of your crossings goes under first, whether your track holds up or turns, and where on the property stays firm no matter what. If there is hardstand near the road or a spot by the shed that never goes soft, tell us. Setting the container down there and letting you shift it in with a tractor when the ground comes good is often the cleanest way through a wet week.

faqs.q: Do you have containers in Mackay or do they come up from Brisbane?
faqs.a: We hold stock at a depot in Mackay, so most local orders go out on a unit that is already here. Not every size and grade is standing locally every week — anything we do not have comes up from our Cornubia yard and adds meaningfully to the date, and you will be told which of those applies at the quote rather than afterwards. You are welcome to inspect before ordering; it simply has to be arranged, because the depot has no public counter and nobody waiting to open up.

faqs.q: Does a shipping container need to be tied down for cyclone season?
faqs.a: If it is going somewhere exposed and will sit empty or lightly loaded, yes. An empty container has a lot of side area and not much mass. Bolting to a slab, cyclone-rated ground anchors with turnbuckles to the corner castings, or poured footings are the usual methods, and which one suits depends on what it is standing on. Where the anchoring has to be certified — a commercial site, or anything an insurer or builder will ask about — get an engineer to specify it. We will not tell you a container is cyclone-rated on its own, because that depends on the anchoring and the load, not the box.

faqs.q: Can you deliver onto a cane farm in the Pioneer Valley?
faqs.a: Regularly. What we need to know is the approach: whether there is a tramway crossing on it and how it sits relative to the road, because a crossing that stands proud with a short run-up will hang a long truck up, and whether the headland gives a real turning area rather than a tractor-sized one. During the crush, haul road and tramway traffic affects timing. If the track will not carry a loaded truck, we set the container on firm ground near the shed or the road and you walk it in with the tractor at your convenience.

faqs.q: How does the wet season affect delivery around Mackay?
faqs.a: In town, hardly at all. Out on the flats and the valley farms it matters a great deal, because heavy river soil that carries a truck comfortably in September will not hold one after a real event, and Mackay rain is not gentle. We will ring and move a booking a couple of days rather than bog a truck on your place. Through summer we leave room in out-of-town runs and keep you posted. When you book, say what your approach crosses and how long those crossings usually stay up.

locations.line: Townsville is a garrison town, a port and a dry-tropics city that gets most of its rain in a handful of weeks, and every one of those facts changes what a container is for and how it should be set up. People arrive on posting and leave again, which puts a floor under storage demand year-round. The port and the corridor west to Mount Isa run on staged gear. And February 2019 taught the whole city something about where water goes that no amount of website copy could.
locations.uses: household storage for defence families mid-posting who need a whole house held somewhere secure between quarters, tool and spares storage for the trades and contractors working out of the Bohle and Stuart industrial estates, staged gear for the businesses supplying the mining corridor west along the Flinders, boat, tinnie and reef gear where the garage never stood a chance, feed and fencing on the grazing country out toward Woodstock and Charters Towers, site stores on the builds through Deeragun, Burdell and Idalia, and dry storage for clubs and community groups
access: Townsville ground is not one thing. Large parts of the suburbs sit on reactive clay that swells and shrinks with the season, and out through Kirwan, Condon, Rasmussen and the Deeragun side that movement is enough to take a container out of square inside a couple of years if there is nothing under the corners. Closer to the water — The Strand, Pallarenda, North Ward, Railway Estate — it goes coastal, sandier and lower, with a shallow water table in places and salt in the air. Then there is Castle Hill and the streets wrapped around it, where the blocks are cut into rock at an angle and the driveways are short, steep and often turn while they climb. That combination is the one that beats a tilt-tray, because the bed grounds on the transition or the truck runs out of driveway before it can straighten. Crane work is common on those blocks and generally the quicker answer. The industrial and defence side is administratively particular rather than technically hard. Base and port work means gate access, identification, escorts, nominated windows and sometimes a specific route on site, all of which are easy to arrange in advance and impossible to arrange at the boom. Stuart, Bohle and the Cleveland Bay industrial area are otherwise straightforward, wide-gated hardstand work. Weather here is its own scheduling factor. The dry tropics are dry for most of the year, which makes ground conditions predictable and delivery easy, and then a monsoon trough parks itself over the city and the rules change completely. In 2019 the water that caused most of the damage came across the ground, not up a river, and blocks through Idalia, Hermit Park, Rosslea and Oonoonba that had never had a problem found out otherwise. That is worth knowing before you choose which corner of the yard the container lives in.

sections.h: Local stock, postings and the run west
p: We hold containers at a depot in Townsville. In a city this far from the eastern seaboard depots, that is the difference between a container being an ordinary purchase and a freight exercise, and it is the reason we can quote Townsville sensibly at all. It also serves a big catchment: the coastal strip north and south, the grazing country inland, and the corridor west along the Flinders where a lot of what goes to Mount Isa and the mines out that way gets staged in a Townsville yard first. It also means a Townsville order behaves like a purchase with a date on it rather than a freight enquiry with a shrug attached, and if something changes — a booking pulled because of weather, a unit that has to come back and be swapped — that is a local trip rather than a fortnight lost.

You can inspect before ordering, arranged in advance rather than dropped in on, because the depot has no public counter and an unannounced visit means a locked gate. Ring, say what you are after, and we will set a time with the unit accessible and someone there while you go over the floor, the seals and the door gear yourself. If getting to the yard does not suit, photos of the specific unit are available on request and we send them before delivery. What is standing locally varies week to week, so if the requirement is specific — high cube, double doors, a particular grade — ask early and you will be told plainly whether it is here or coming north.

sections.h: Wind, anchoring and what a container is not
p: Townsville is cyclone country and the building rules here reflect that, so it is a fair question and it deserves a straight answer. A shipping container is a strong, well-built steel box, but its behaviour in a serious wind event has far more to do with how it is anchored and how heavily it is loaded than with the box itself. Empty and standing in an exposed position, it presents a very large side area against not much weight. Loaded, and held down properly, it is a different object entirely. If a unit is going somewhere open and will sit empty for stretches, it needs to be restrained: bolted to a slab, held with cyclone-rated ground anchors and turnbuckles at the corner castings, or set on poured footings.

Where the restraint has to be certified — anything on a commercial site, anything forming part of a build, anything an insurer will want documented — that specification comes from an engineer and not from a delivery driver or a website. We will set a container up properly, we will tell you what we have seen work in this district, and we will tell you where the line is. What you will not get from us is a claim that the container is rated on its own, because that is not how it works and it is exactly the sort of assurance that costs somebody a shed roof in February. It is worth a walk around the unit before the season too. Loose sheeting leaned against the side, a tarp tied to a corner casting, stacked pallets and anything bolted on as an awning are the parts that let go first, and they are all easier to deal with in October than in the middle of a warning.

sections.h: The dry, the wet and where the water goes
p: For most of the year Townsville is about as predictable as delivery gets. The ground is dry, the surfaces are firm, and a truck can go where it needs to go. Then the trough arrives and the district takes a season of rain in a week. The lesson of 2019 was that the damage largely came from water moving across the ground rather than from a river rising in the usual way, which means the useful question about your block is not just how high it is but which way water crosses it when it has nowhere else to go. Most people know the answer without being asked. You have watched it happen off the neighbour's driveway or down the side of the house in a big storm, and that observation is worth more than any map for deciding which corner of the yard the container lives in.

For a container, the guidance is simple and worth being blunt about. It is not a flood barrier and it should never be sold as one. Water reaching the door sill gets past the seals and into the box, and an empty container floats, which is precisely the scenario in which it does damage to someone else's fence rather than staying where you left it. So put it on the highest usable ground, keep it out of the flow path, and if there is no high ground, raise the floor on blocks or a built pad so the sill sits well clear. Anchoring matters here for two reasons at once — wind and buoyancy — which is a good argument for doing it properly the first time.

faqs.q: Do you have containers in Townsville, or does everything come from down south?
faqs.a: We hold stock at a depot in Townsville, which is why local orders usually run to a two to four day window rather than a freight timeline. Not every size and grade is standing here in a given week, and anything we do not have comes north from the Cornubia yard and takes noticeably longer — you will be told which applies at the quote. If you want to see one first, ring and we will arrange it; the depot is not a retail yard and there is nobody there to open up on spec.

faqs.q: Can you get a container across to Magnetic Island?
faqs.a: Yes, though the final leg travels on a barge, and what that barge will take — length, weight, loading, running times — is the operator's call rather than something we can promise on a web page. Those terms move, so we sort them out with the operator while your job is being priced and give you one answer that covers the container and getting it over the water. A 20ft is considerably easier to shift across and place on an island block than a 40ft. Tell us the street and describe the block.

faqs.q: Does a container need tying down for cyclone season in Townsville?
faqs.a: If it is exposed and will sit empty or lightly loaded, yes. An empty container has a large side area against relatively little mass. Options are bolting to a slab, cyclone-rated ground anchors with turnbuckles to the corner castings, or poured footings, and which one suits depends on what it is standing on. Anything that has to be certified — a commercial site, part of a build, or something an insurer will ask about — needs an engineer to specify it. We will not claim the container is rated on its own, because performance comes from the anchoring and the load.

faqs.q: My driveway off Castle Hill is short and steep. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Often, but usually not with a tilt-tray. A drive that climbs and turns at the same time, or that changes grade sharply at the kerb, will ground the rear of the bed before the container has slid clear, and there is no technique that gets around it. On those blocks a crane truck standing in the street and lifting over the fence or the carport is the practical method and it goes in first time. Send one photo from the road looking up the drive and another from the spot looking back down it, and we will name the truck before anything is booked.
